# Sarah's Vigilance

Sarah sits at her desk in the climate-controlled server room of a mid-sized tech firm, her fingers moving across the keyboard with practiced efficiency. At twenty-one, she's already established herself as a reliable database administrator, the kind of employee who catches errors others miss and maintains systems with meticulous attention. But beneath her professional competence runs a current of tension that never quite releases.

Three years ago, Sarah was working as a junior intelligence analyst for the military, stationed in a forward operating base in the Middle East. She was good at the work—pattern recognition, data analysis, the careful construction of intelligence reports. She felt purposeful, contributing to something larger than herself. On a routine morning in October, a mortar attack struck the base. Sarah was in the administrative building when the first impact hit, close enough that she felt the concussive force push through her chest. The subsequent explosions came in rapid succession. She remembers the sound more than anything—a roaring that seemed to come from everywhere at once. She remembers the dust so thick she couldn't see her own hands. She remembers the screaming, though she was never entirely sure if some of it came from her own throat.

Three soldiers were killed that day. Sarah wasn't injured physically, though a piece of shrapnel passed so close to her head that it singed her hair. She was medically discharged six months later, not because of visible wounds but because of what the military psychiatrist called "severe combat-related stress."

Now, at her desk, Sarah's body remains hypervigilant in ways her conscious mind struggles to control. Loud noises make her flinch—the printer jamming, a colleague's raised voice in the hallway, even the coffee machine's hiss can send her heart racing. Last week, a car backfired in the parking lot, and she found herself under her desk before she'd fully registered what had happened. Her coworker had found her there, shaking, unable to explain why she'd reacted that way. She'd told him it was just a startle response, nothing serious.

Sleep remains fragmented and unreliable. Most nights, Sarah lies awake until two or three in the morning, her mind cycling through scenarios—what if she'd been in a different building, what if the attack had come at a different time, what if she hadn't survived. When she does sleep, she dreams of the base, but the details shift and distort. Sometimes she's trapped in the rubble. Sometimes she's watching it happen to someone else and can't move to help. She wakes gasping, her sheets soaked with sweat, and spends the remaining hours until dawn scrolling through her phone or working on database queries from home—anything to keep her mind occupied.

At work, Sarah maintains meticulous control. She arrives early, leaves late, and rarely takes breaks. Her supervisor praises her dedication, unaware that Sarah's rigid routine is a form of self-protection. She needs to know exactly what's happening around her at all times. She sits with her back to the wall whenever possible. She maps exits in every room. She monitors her coworkers' movements, tracking who's where, assessing potential threats. This hypervigilance exhausts her, but the alternative—relaxing, trusting that nothing bad will happen—feels impossibly dangerous.

Sarah hasn't told anyone at her civilian job about her military service or her discharge. She's twenty-one years old and already feels separated from her peers by an invisible gulf. They talk about weekend plans and dating and student loans, and Sarah nods along while internally calculating risk assessments and monitoring the room for exits. She's become skilled at appearing fine, at performing normalcy. But beneath the surface, she remains stationed in that moment of impact, waiting for the next explosion.
